introduction-speed-vs-safety.core: Manual review by a central team doesn't scale: either it becomes a bottleneck or reviewers rubber-stamp. Policy as code turns rules ("no public buckets", "prod instances need tags", "no deleting databases") into machine-checked code that runs automatically on every change. Teams move fast within guardrails, and exceptions are explicit and audited.

first_principles.problem: A security team reviewing every Terraform PR has a three-day queue, so teams find ways around it.
truths: Rules can be expressed as code.

analogy.title: Guardrails on a mountain road
analogy.story: Drivers go at speed because the rails stop them going over the edge, without a police officer at every bend.
analogy.breaks: Guardrails are physical; policies only cover rules someone wrote.

example.title: Rule journey
flow: Policy: deny if public ACL or no public access block

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Review queue gone; rules applied 100% of the time.

check.q: What's the main benefit of policy as code over manual review?
check.a: Rules are applied consistently and instantly to every change, removing the bottleneck while keeping safety.

static-analysis-checkov-and-tfsec.core: Checkov and Trivy (which absorbed tfsec) ship hundreds of built-in checks mapped to CIS and other benchmarks. They scan Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes and Dockerfiles for misconfigurations. They're the fastest policy layer, requiring no custom code, and support inline skips with justification. They can scan plan JSON too, for resolved values.

first_principles.problem: A team wants immediate security coverage without writing any policies themselves.

analogy.title: A home inspector's standard checklist
analogy.story: They check the same hundred known hazards in every house without you writing the list.
analogy.breaks: Inspectors use judgement; scanners flag everything that matches.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Real findings fail CI; approved exceptions are documented.

check.q: Why include a reason in a Checkov skip comment?
check.a: It documents why the exception is acceptable and makes it auditable, rather than silently suppressing a finding.

opa-and-rego-the-universal-policy-engine.core: Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose engine: you give it JSON input (a Terraform plan, a Kubernetes admission request, an API call) and Rego policies, and it returns decisions. Because it is tool-agnostic, the same engine and language serve Terraform (conftest), Kubernetes (Gatekeeper), CI, and microservice authorisation, giving one policy skill set across the stack.

first_principles.problem: Each tool has its own policy syntax, so the security team maintains rules in five languages.
truths: Decisions can be decoupled from tools.

analogy.title: A universal judge
analogy.story: Any case file in a standard format can be brought to the same judge applying the same law book.
analogy.breaks: Judges interpret; OPA evaluates logic exactly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One engine for infra, k8s and app authz.

code.text:
# Terraform plan
conftest test plan.json -p policy/
# Kubernetes manifests in CI
conftest test k8s/*.yaml -p policy/
# Live API decision
curl -s localhost:8181/v1/data/authz/allow -d '{"input": {"user": "ana", "action": "delete"}}'

check.a: It evaluates policies against any JSON input and is decoupled from the tool, so the same engine serves Terraform, Kubernetes, CI and APIs.

learning-rego-syntax.core: Rego is declarative: rules are true when all their body expressions are true, and iteration is implicit through variables that bind to values satisfying the conditions. Partial set rules (`deny contains msg if {...}`) collect every violation. Key tools are `some ... in` for iteration, `every` for universal checks, helper functions, and `opa test` for unit-testing policies with fixture inputs.

first_principles.problem: An engineer writes Rego like Python loops and gets confusing results that never trigger.

analogy.title: A database query, not a script
analogy.story: You describe which rows you want and the engine finds them; you don't write the loop.
analogy.breaks: SQL has tables; Rego navigates nested JSON.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Collects one message per non-compliant resource; tested with opa test.

check.q: In Rego, what does defining the same rule twice with different bodies mean?
check.a: Logical OR: the rule is true if either body is satisfied.

hashicorp-sentinel-enterprise-integrated.core: Sentinel is HashiCorp's embedded policy language in HCP Terraform/Enterprise (and Vault, Consul, Nomad). Policies run between plan and apply with imports such as tfplan/v2, tfconfig and tfstate, plus cost estimates. Enforcement levels are advisory (warn), soft-mandatory (override allowed with permission) or hard-mandatory (block). It integrates tightly but only in HashiCorp's commercial products; HCP Terraform also supports OPA.

first_principles.problem: A company on Terraform Enterprise needs cost and security gates that some admins can override with a record.
derivation: Use **tfrun** for cost and workspace context.

analogy.title: A building's integrated access system
analogy.story: Badges, cameras and override keys are built in, but only work inside that building.
analogy.breaks: Buildings are physical; policies can be ported if written in OPA instead.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Runs adding >$500/month need an authorised override.

code.text:
import "tfrun"
import "decimal"

limit = decimal.new(500)
main = rule {
  decimal.new(tfrun.cost_estimate.delta_monthly_cost).less_than(limit)
}
# policy set: enforcement_level = "soft-mandatory"

check.q: What does soft-mandatory mean in Sentinel?
check.a: The policy blocks by default, but a user with permission can override it, and the override is logged.

where-does-it-fit-in-the-pipeline.core: Run policies at several points: in the IDE and pre-commit for instant feedback (Checkov, TFLint); in PR CI on code and plan JSON (conftest, Checkov); at the platform gate between plan and apply (Sentinel/OPA in HCP Terraform or Spacelift); at Kubernetes admission (Gatekeeper, Kyverno); and continuously at runtime (AWS Config, Security Hub) to catch drift and click-ops.

first_principles.problem: Policies only run in CI, so a console change creating a public bucket is never caught.

analogy.title: Layers of airport security
analogy.story: Online check-in rules, bag drop, security scan, gate check and on-board crew each catch different things.
analogy.breaks: Airports have one entry path; infra has many, including the console.

example.title: Same rule, four layers
flow: Runtime: AWS Config rule s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited + auto-remediation

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Caught early normally, caught late if bypassed.

check.q: Why add runtime policy checks if CI already enforces rules?
check.a: Changes can bypass the pipeline (console, scripts, other tools), and only runtime monitoring catches those.
